style: calm, natural hesitations, like explaining to a friend
slides: Okay, before you practice, here's a quick summary of probability.
Everything important, one idea at a time.
Probability is wanted over possible. And you count outcomes that are equally likely.
Three red and seven yellow counters. So three red out of ten... three tenths.
A probability is always between zero and one. Zero is impossible, one is certain. Got more than one? Then something went wrong.
Always start from the bottom. What can happen?
A student from the choir is chosen? Then the bottom is the fifteen choir students. Not all thirty-two students.
Something was already taken out? Count the bag as it is now.
And past results don't change a fair coin. Four heads in a row... the next toss is still one half.
Now, the complement. Something either happens or it doesn't. Together, that's one.
Red is five twelfths? Then blue is seven twelfths.
Sometimes the opposite is easier to count. Late trains are one fifth. So on time is four fifths.
But answer what they asked. One fifth is the late trap.
AND means multiply. Heads, and a three on a dice? One half times one sixth... one twelfth.
OR means add. But only for cases that can't happen together. A one or a four? One sixth plus one sixth.
Can they happen together? Then subtract the overlap once. From one to thirty, divisible by three or five? Ten, plus six, minus two.
And a second try only happens after a first miss. So it's one fifth, plus four fifths times one quarter... two fifths.
At least one? Too many cases. So count the opposite, none, and subtract it from one.
Two coins, at least one head? One minus a quarter, three quarters. Not one half plus one half... that counts two heads twice.
Exactly one head in four tosses? One order is one sixteenth. There are four orders, so four sixteenths... one quarter.
Two drawn together? Treat it as one after the other, without replacement.
Two stages, first a bag, then a token? Draw a tree.
Along a branch it's AND, so multiply. Different branches are OR, so add.
And don't pour the bags together. Different sizes mean different chances.
Also, watch for stages that depend on each other. Whoever wins the first prize can't win the second.
Three coins all land the same way? Well, the first one can be anything. That's one. The other two must match it. One half times one half... one quarter.
And you're allowed to choose the order. Start with the stage that can't go wrong.
One red marble out of nine. Is it first, third, or last? It's always one ninth.
With two dice, ten and four are the same distance from seven. So they have the same probability. Dice with n faces? Then the top sum, the most likely one, is n plus one.
Letters in the choices? Plug in small numbers. But first check that the four choices come out different.
So, before you start, always ask yourself these questions.
And the traps: adding when you should use one minus none, pouring two bags together, and giving the complement instead of what they asked.
Okay, now it's your turn. Good luck.
